newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Major traders aim for quick infotech pact agreement.
newsitem.headline: Major traders aim for quick infotech pact agreement.

text.p: The European Union (EU) along with the United States, Canada and Japan, were making progress on Tuesday in solving differences over a global pact on free trade in information technology, a senior EU official said.

There were hopes for further advances in talks later in the day toward an Information Technology Agreement (ITA), the main goal of this first ministerial meeting of the fledgling World Trade Organisation (WTO), EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan told reporters.
"We are making a lot of progress and we hope to make further progress this afternoon," Brittan said after after a luncheon meeting of the four major trading partners.

Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefksy said she concurred with Brittan's comments, but declined to say anything more on the proposed pact to eliminate tariffs on an estimated $600 billion worth of computer products by 2000.

"There is no question that what the industrialised countries now hope for most here is a deal on information technology products and agreement to work hard for a basic telecommunications pact by February," said one key negotiator.

Signals from negotiators left little doubt the major traders were aiming for agreement as quickly as possible -- perhaps by Wednesday -- to convince Asian trading partners to sign on to the agreement by the end of this week's meeting.

Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told the second day of the Conference he hoped "ardently....that we will have an agreement as the most significant achievement of this ministerial conference in the area of trade liberalisation."
However, several Asian nations have voiced reservations, with Malaysia saying the goal of free commerce in infotech by the turn of the century is too ambitious.
Malaysia opposed negotiating the pact and said it did not see agreement by the close of this week's meeting on Friday.
"We did not come here to discuss the Information Technology Agreement," international trade and industry minister Rafidah Aziz told reporters. "All negotiations should be done in Geneva."

The 128 full delegations from WTO member countries and ministers and officials from nearly 30 others waiting to be admitted to the organisation have also heard ringing appeals for progress to a telecoms liberalisation pact.

Negotiators at WTO headquarters in Geneva are facing a deadline to finalise a deal among some 50 countries by mid-February after failing in an earlier bid last April when the United States pulled out of the talks.
This sector, heavily protected in many emerging economies is estimated to be worth well over $500 billion annually.

As the full conference entered its second day on Tuesday, key ministers and their aides from different areas of the globe met in conclave to try to hammer out the final text of a declaration to be issued at the end of the gathering on Friday.

Sixteen of 20 paragraphs have been agreed, but there was no doubt a major battle was under way over the last four -- touching mainly on the "new issues" such as labour standards, corruption in trade and competition and investment that have proved the most divisive in Singapore.

Officials said negotiating on whether the declaration, meant to point the WTO down the free trade path into the 21st century, should include any reference at all to the labour issue was being left to last.

Several key emerging economies in Asia -- including India, Malaysia and Indonesia -- are insisting there should be no mention at all, arguing that even a neutral phrasing would suggest work conditions were a subject for the WTO.
